Reticent

/RET-ih-suhnt/ - the stress falls on RET · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Reticent means hesitant to speak up; keeping one's thoughts to oneself.

Grandpa stayed reticent about his years at sea; asked directly, he would nod at the horizon and change the subject.

Worked Example

Three lunches into her first week, all anyone at the workshop knew about Imani was that she kept bees — and that only because a jar of honey had appeared on the break table with a small handwritten label. She answered questions warmly and briefly, asked better ones back, and returned to her sandwich. The crew liked her enormously and knew almost nothing about her.

Reticent is the exact word for Imani, because it means hesitant to speak up, keeping one's thoughts to oneself — the silence is chosen, comfortable, and aimed mostly at her own affairs. Guarded would imply wariness, something protected; reticence needs no threat at all, only a preference.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tight-lipped: clamped shut on one subject in particular

guarded: careful about what gets out — weighing every word for risk

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

talkative: the chatter flows freely on any topic

forthcoming: offers information before being pressed

Where it sits · how much of oneself stays held back — private → reticent → walled-off

private vs. reticent: Private is the mild preference — a few doors politely closed, plenty still shared.

walled-off vs. reticent: Walled-off goes further than reticent — a reticent colleague still answers when pressed, while a walled-off one lets nothing through at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: thoroughly (an intensifier)

Root — tic-

Root — tic-: to be silent (Latin tacere; the a thins to i inside compounds)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (an intensifier: thoroughly) + tic- (to be silent) + -ent = in a state of thorough silence. Latin reticere was tacere, 'to be silent,' compounded and strengthened; the reticent hold their silence deliberately, keeping thoughts in rather than letting them out. No repetition anywhere in the word — re-'s third job again.

The silent root you'll meet elsewhere

The silent root you'll meet elsewhere: Reticent grows from Latin tacere, 'to be silent' — a root English did keep, in tacit (understood without being said) and taciturn (silent by temperament), both taught elsewhere in this course. This card leaves them to their own lessons; notice only that re- adds no repetition here — just silence, thorough and chosen.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / restrained

Reticent describes people, and their manner, when thoughts stay unspoken: answers short, opinions unoffered. Tight-lipped is the informal twin, usually about one topic; guarded adds wariness. Two boundaries matter: reluctant — a cousin in this unit's reference list — is unwillingness to act, while reticence is unwillingness to speak; and recalcitrant, this unit's louder mate, refuses authority outright. The reticent refuse nothing; they simply are not saying.
